claim: Heterozygous loss of human PAFAH1B1 (coding for LIS1) results in the disruption of neurogenesis and neuronal migration via dysregulation of microtubule (MT) stability and dynein motor function/localization that alters mitotic spindle orientation, chromosomal segregation, and nuclear migration.

claim: Human-induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models revealed an important role for LIS1 in controlling the length of terminal cell divisions of outer radial glial (oRG) progenitors.

evidence: This statement references recent iPSC model findings, suggesting it is based on prior published work.

claim: Lissencephaly (smooth brain) is a brain malformation disorder associated with haploinsufficiency of Lissencephaly-1 (LIS1), also called PAFAH1B1.
source: Lissencephaly (smooth brain) is a brain malformation disorder associated with haploinsufficiency of Lissencephaly-1 (LIS1), also called PAFAH1B1 (Platelet-activating factor acetylhydrolase IB subunit alpha) (Dobyns et al., 1993; Hattori et al., 1994; Reiner et al., 1993; Moon and Wynshaw-Boris, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: LIS1 is an important regulatory protein controlling cytoplasmic dynein and microtubules.
source: At the molecular level, LIS1 is an important regulatoratory protein controlling cytoplasmic dynein and microtubules (MTs), that is also known to have dual roles coordinating both MTs and the actin cytoskeleton (Kholmanskikh et al., 2003; Kholmanskikh et al., 2006; Jheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LIS1 has dual roles coordinating both MTs and the actin cytoskeleton.
source: At the molecular level, LIS1 is an important regulatoratory protein controlling cytoplasmic dynein and microtubules (MTs), that is also known to have dual roles coordinating both MTs and the actin cytoskeleton (Kholmanskikh et al., 2003; Kholmanskikh et al., 2006; Jheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pafah1b1 mouse mutant studies suggest additional cellular functions of LIS1 in neocortical neural progenitor cell (NPC) division by regulating mitotic spindle orientation and cell fate.

evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior mouse mutant studies.

claim: The mitotic phenotypes of Pafah1b1 mutants are closely related and consistent with those of other mutants of MT/dynein-associated proteins such as LGN, NDE1, and NDEL1.
source: The mitotic phenotypes of Pafah1b1 mutants are closely related and consistent with those of other mutants of MT/dynein-associated proteins such as LGN, NDE1, and NDEL1 (Bradshaw and Hayashi, 2017; Doobin et al., 2016; Wynne and Vallee, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations comparing phenotypes across different mutants.

evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent iPSC study.

evidence: This is established knowledge about Miller-Dieker syndrome.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on RhoA function.

claim: When coordination between MTs and F-actin is perturbed, abnormally fewer or elongated astral MTs destabilize the cleavage furrow.

This MT dysfunction induces actomyosin dysregulation, leading to cell membrane hyper-contractility, RhoA and F-actin mislocalization outside of the midzone/cleavage furrow, cell shape oscillation, and subsequent mitotic failure (Canman et al., 2003; Murthy and Wadsworth, 2008; Rankin and Wordeman, 2010; Watanabe et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on MT-actin coordination.

source: In the WT-MADM neocortex, Anillin was accumulated at the midzone during metaphase-to-anaphase (Figure 1A–a,b) and was enriched by forming a 'U' shape (basal-to-apical ingression) at the midbody of NPCs, consistent with previous observations of normal NPC cleavage in WT mice (Kosodo et al., 2008; Figure 1A–c,d).
